title: A Gallery of Matrices
intro: Every matrix that the two viewers offer, one after another: what each picture shows, the eigenvalues and eigenvectors as the readout prints them, what to try, and the one thing each matrix teaches. Thirteen live in the plane and ten in space.

blocks.text: How to use this page

Each entry below is a full viewer, set to one preset, so you can leave it on this page and experiment: nothing you do to one affects the others. Every one has the same controls. Matrix A swaps the matrix (the gallery's choice is only the starting point), Direction of v turns the probe, Powers shown, k adds the dots for $A^kv$, and Next step ▶ walks through the eight steps in order. The three-dimensional ones add v: direction around, v: direction up, Turn and Tilt, or drag the picture.

The numbers quoted are what the readout under each viewer prints at the settings given. If you want the reasons behind them, the pages are Directions a Matrix Keeps (#/math/eigenvalues/invariant-directions), Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/math/eigenvalues/finding-eigenvalues), Diagonalisation and Powers (#/math/eigenvalues/diagonalisation), Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem (#/math/eigenvalues/symmetric-matrices), Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues) and Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues); the formulas are collected on Eigenvalue Tables (#/math/eigenvalues/tables). Eigenvectors in the viewers are printed as unit vectors with two decimals, and the sign of a vector is a free choice.
Stretches and symmetric matrices
Stretch: diag(2, 0.5)

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: The simplest matrix there is: it stretches $x$ by 2 and squeezes $y$ by a half. The eigenvectors are the axes themselves, $\lambda_1 = 2$ along $(1, 0)$ and $\lambda_2 = 0.5$ along $(0, 1)$, because a diagonal matrix multiplies each coordinate on its own. The unit circle becomes an upright ellipse with half-widths 2 and 0.5. The determinant is $2 \times 0.5 = 1$, so areas are unchanged even though shapes are not. At 20° the probe $v$ goes to $(1.88, 0.17)$, length 1.887, turned $-14.8°$: every vector off the axes is dragged towards the $x$-axis because that is where the stretch is bigger.

Set Powers shown, k to 5. The readout ends 'A^5v = (30.07, 0.01), length 30.07, 0.02° from the λ₁ line': the $y$-part has been multiplied by $0.5^5 = 0.031$ and the $x$-part by $2^5 = 32$. Then move Direction of v to 90°: the probe sits on the teal line and the dots never leave it. What it teaches: a diagonal matrix is the case every other matrix is trying to become, by a change of basis.

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: Here the eigenvectors are $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$, with $\lambda_1 = 3$ and $\lambda_2 = 1$, and they are perpendicular. The ellipse is tilted $45°$ with its long half-axis 3 along the blue line and its short half-axis 1 along the teal line. At 20° the readout says $Av = (2.22, 1.62)$, length 2.752, turned $16.2°$: it is pulled towards $45°$. The trace is 4 and the determinant 3, so $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 3)$.

Press Next step ▶ until step 5 and the walk-through text above the readout notes that the two directions are perpendicular, 'as they always are for a symmetric matrix'. Press Sweep v: the green 'along' curve in the top-right panel rises to 3 at 45° and falls to 1 at 135°, and it never leaves the band between 1 and 3. Those are the Rayleigh quotient's limits. What it teaches: for a symmetric matrix the eigenvectors are the axes of the picture (see Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem (#/math/eigenvalues/symmetric-matrices)).
Not symmetric: [[4, 1], [2, 3]]

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: The matrix of the worked examples: $\lambda_1 = 5$ along $(0.71, 0.71)$ and $\lambda_2 = 2$ along $(-0.45, 0.89)$, the direction $(1, -2)$. The two eigen-lines are $71.6°$ apart, not $90°$. The ellipse is still tilted, but its axes are no longer along the eigen-lines: the dashed lines pass through the ellipse at an angle. At 20° the probe goes to $(4.10, 2.91)$, length 5.026, turned $15.3°$. The determinant 10 is the area factor, $5 \times 2$.

Compare with the symmetric preset above. Step through Next step ▶ to step 5, where the text says the two directions are $71.6°$ apart, 'not perpendicular: A is not symmetric'. Turn Direction of v until $Av$ lies on the teal line (about 117°) and then to the blue line (45°): both are eigen-directions even though the ellipse's long axis is elsewhere. Set Powers shown, k to 3 and Direction of v to 0° to see the numbers of Power Iteration and Markov Chains (#/math/eigenvalues/power-iteration). What it teaches: eigenvectors need not be perpendicular, and are not the axes of the ellipse.
A negative eigenvalue: [[1, 2], [2, −2]]

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: Trace $-1$ and determinant $-6$ give $\lambda^2 + \lambda - 6 = (\lambda + 3)(\lambda - 2)$, so $\lambda_1 = -3$ along $(-0.45, 0.89)$ and $\lambda_2 = 2$ along $(0.89, 0.45)$. The largest in size is $-3$, so it is listed first and drawn blue. Along the blue line a vector is tripled and reversed: its thick arrow $\lambda v$ points the opposite way from $v$. The matrix is symmetric, so the lines are perpendicular. At 20° the probe goes to $(1.62, 1.20)$, length 2.016.

Move Direction of v to 117° (the blue line is at 116.6°) and watch $Av$ flip to the other side of the origin. In the sweep panel the 'along' curve at the blue line is $-3$, the eigenvalue itself, a negative number. The determinant is negative, which is why the image of the unit square is mirrored, not just turned. What it teaches: a negative eigenvalue means 'stretch and reverse', and a negative determinant means 'reflect'.
Matrices that generate sequences

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: The matrix takes the pair $(F_{n+1}, F_n)$ to $(F_{n+1} + F_n, F_{n+1}) = (F_{n+2}, F_{n+1})$, so its powers generate the Fibonacci numbers. Its eigenvalues are the roots of $\lambda^2 - \lambda - 1 = 0$: $\lambda_1 = \varphi = 1.618$ along $(0.85, 0.53)$ and $\lambda_2 = -0.618$ along $(-0.53, 0.85)$. The negative one is smaller in size, so in the powers it fades while alternating in sign.

The preset starts at Direction of v = 0° with Powers shown, k = 8. The readout ends 'A^8v = (34.00, 21.00), length 39.962, 0.02° from the λ₁ line': that is $(F_9, F_8)$, and $34/21 = 1.619$ is already within $0.001$ of $\varphi = 1.618$. Drag k from 1 to 8 and the dots 1, 2, 3, … hop across the blue line (because of the negative $\lambda_2$) with each hop smaller than the last. What it teaches: the ratio of neighbouring Fibonacci numbers is a power-iteration estimate of the dominant eigenvalue (see Diagonalisation and Powers (#/math/eigenvalues/diagonalisation)).

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: The weather chain of Power Iteration and Markov Chains (#/math/eigenvalues/power-iteration): columns sum to 1, so $\lambda_1 = 1$ along $(0.89, 0.45)$, the steady state $(2, 1)/3$ once scaled to sum 1, and $\lambda_2 = 0.7$ along $(0.71, -0.71)$. The trace is 1.7 and the determinant 0.7, which is $1 \times 0.7$ as it must be.

The preset starts at Direction of v = 0° (so $v = (1, 0)$, 'certainly sunny') with Powers shown, k = 10. The readout ends 'A^10v = (0.68, 0.32), length 0.75, 0.97° from the λ₁ line'. The first two numbers are the probabilities after 10 days. Drag k up and down: each step closes about 30 per cent of the remaining gap. What it teaches: a stochastic matrix has an eigenvalue 1 and the steady state is its eigenvector.
Flips and projections
Reflection across y = x

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: Swapping the coordinates mirrors the plane across the line $y = x$. A vector on the mirror is unchanged, $\lambda = 1$ along $(0.71, 0.71)$, and a vector perpendicular to it is reversed, $\lambda = -1$ along $(0.71, -0.71)$. Trace 0, determinant $-1$. Lengths are preserved, so the image of the circle is the circle itself: the green ellipse covers the dashed one. At 20° the probe goes to $(0.34, 0.94)$, still length 1, but turned $50°$, which is twice the $25°$ between $v$ and the mirror.

Drag Direction of v and watch the readout's 'turned' value: it is always twice the angle from $v$ to the mirror, so it reads 0° at 45° (on the mirror) and −180° at 135° (perpendicular to it, where $Av = -v$). Set Powers shown, k to 3: the dots jump between two directions, $v$ and its mirror image, and never settle, because $|\lambda_1| = |\lambda_2|$. What it teaches: $-1$ is an eigenvalue of every reflection, and equal sizes mean power iteration cannot choose.
Projection onto the x-axis

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: Throw away the $y$-coordinate: $(x, y) \to (x, 0)$. The $x$-axis stays put, $\lambda_1 = 1$ along $(1, 0)$, and the $y$-axis is crushed to the origin, $\lambda_2 = 0$ along $(0, 1)$. The determinant is 0, and the unit circle becomes a flat segment from $-1$ to $1$: the green ellipse has no height. At 20° $Av = (0.94, 0.00)$, length 0.94, turned $-20°$. Applying it twice does nothing new, $A^2 = A$, which is why a projection can only have eigenvalues 0 and 1.

Move Direction of v and watch $Av$ slide along the $x$-axis only. At 90° the arrow vanishes: $Av = (0, 0)$, length 0. In the polynomial panel $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - \lambda$ has roots 0 and 1. What it teaches: an eigenvalue 0 is a direction the matrix kills, and the matrix has no inverse.
Rotations and spirals
Rotation by 30°

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: A rotation sends every direction to another direction, so no real line survives. The readout says 'no real eigenvalues: λ = 0.866 ± 0.5j, size |λ| = 1 and angle 30°, so A turns every vector'. The numbers are $\cos 30° = 0.866$ and $\sin 30° = 0.5$, and the pair $\cos\theta \pm j\sin\theta$ has size 1 and angle $30°$. The image of the circle is the circle. The polynomial $\lambda^2 - 1.732\lambda + 1$ never touches zero. At 20° the probe goes to $(0.64, 0.77)$, length 1, turned exactly $30°$.

Press Sweep v: the 'sideways' curve in the top panel is the constant $\sin 30° = 0.5$ at every angle and never crosses zero, which is what 'no eigen-direction' looks like. Set Powers shown, k to 6: the dots step round by 30° each time and the sixth lands on the opposite side, $A^6v = (-0.94, -0.34) = -v$, length 1. The page Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues) explains the pair.
Rotate and grow: [[1, −1], [1, 1]]

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: The same idea with scaling: $\lambda = 1 \pm 1j$, size $\sqrt{2} = 1.414$, angle $45°$. Each application turns by $45°$ and multiplies the length by $1.414$. The image of the circle is a circle of radius 1.414. At 20° the probe goes to $(0.60, 1.28)$, length 1.414, turned $45°$.

Set Powers shown, k to 8: eight turns of $45°$ make exactly one full revolution and the length is $1.414^8 = 16$. The readout ends 'A^8v = (15.04, 5.47), length 16', which is $16v$ for $v$ at 20°. Drag k from 1 to 8 and the dots go once round the circle; they show directions only, and the growth is in the readout's length, which is multiplied by 1.414 at every step. What it teaches: $|\lambda| > 1$ with an angle is a growing spiral.

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: The same picture with $|\lambda| < 1$: $\lambda = 0.8 \pm 0.3j$, size $0.854$, angle $20.6°$. Each application turns the vector by $20.6°$ and shrinks it to $0.854$ of its length. At 20° the probe goes to $(0.65, 0.56)$, length 0.854. The trace is 1.6 and the determinant $0.73 = 0.854^2$.

Set Powers shown, k to 10. The readout ends 'A^10v = (−0.15, −0.15), length 0.207': ten steps of $20.6°$ turn the vector $206°$ (about half way round) and shrink it to $0.854^{10} = 0.207$ of its length. Raise k step by step and the dots circle slowly while the length falls: a stable spiral, the shape of a damped oscillation or a decaying system (see Eigenvalues in Practice (#/math/eigenvalues/applications)).
Defective and scalar matrices

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: A shear slides each horizontal layer sideways by an amount proportional to its height. The readout says 'one repeated eigenvalue λ = 1, but only one eigen-direction, (1.00, 0.00): the matrix is defective'. The $x$-axis is carried onto itself; every other direction is tilted a little towards it. The area is unchanged (determinant 1). At 20° the probe goes to $(1.28, 0.34)$, length 1.327, turned only $-5.1°$.

Press Sweep v and look at the 'sideways' curve in the top-right panel: it dips to $-1$ at 90° and comes back up to touch zero at 0° and 180° without crossing it. That touch, with no crossing, is the signature of the repeated root. The polynomial graph $\lambda^2 - 2\lambda + 1$ touches zero at $\lambda = 1$. Set Powers shown, k to 10 and see how slowly the dots creep towards the $x$-axis. See Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues).
Scaling 1.5I

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: Multiply every vector by 1.5. The readout says 'one repeated eigenvalue λ = 1.5, and every vector is an eigenvector: A is 1.5 times the identity'. Again a repeated root $\lambda = 1.5$ (the polynomial is $(\lambda - 1.5)^2$), but here the eigenvectors fill the whole plane, not a single line. The determinant is $2.25$ and the image of the circle is a circle of radius 1.5. At 20° the probe goes to $(1.41, 0.51)$, length 1.5, turned $0°$.

Sweep v: the 'sideways' curve is zero for every angle and the 'along' curve is a flat line at 1.5. Compare with the shear above, which has the same trace-and-determinant pattern ($\lambda = 1$ twice) but only one direction. What it teaches: repeated eigenvalue does not tell you whether the matrix is defective; you must count the eigenvectors.
In space

The remaining ten are 3×3. In each, the readout begins with the eigenvalues and then gives the probe and its image; unless an entry says otherwise, the probe starts at around 30° and up 25°, which is $v = (0.78, 0.45, 0.42)$.
Diagonal: diag(2, 1, 0.5)

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: The three-dimensional stretch: eigenvalues $2, 1, 0.5$ along the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes. The unit sphere becomes an ellipsoid with half-lengths 2, 1 and 0.5 along the axes, and the determinant $2 \times 1 \times 0.5 = 1$. The readout: 'λ = 2, along (1.00, 0.00, 0.00); λ = 1, along (0.00, 1.00, 0.00); λ = 0.5, along (0.00, 0.00, 1.00)'. The probe goes to $(1.57, 0.45, 0.21)$, length 1.647, $22.1°$ off its own line.

Press Next step ▶ to step 3 and see the three dashed lines coincide with the axes. In step 7 (which sets k = 8) the numbered dots of the powers swing towards the $x$-axis, the line with the biggest $\lambda$. What it teaches: diagonal means that the axes are the eigenvectors, and the diagonal entries are the eigenvalues.

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: The matrix solved in full on Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/math/eigenvalues/finding-eigenvalues): eigenvalues $2 + \sqrt{2} = 3.414$, $2$ and $2 - \sqrt{2} = 0.586$, with the readout vectors $(0.50, 0.71, 0.50)$, $(0.71, 0.00, -0.71)$ and $(-0.50, 0.71, -0.50)$. They are mutually perpendicular. The probe goes to $(2.02, 2.11, 1.30)$, length 3.201, $14.8°$ off.

The cubic printed at the bottom left is $\lambda^3 - 6\lambda^2 + 10\lambda - 4$, which the graph shows crossing zero at 0.586, 2 and 3.414. Drag the picture to look along each eigen-line in turn: the green ellipsoid is longest along the first and shortest along the third. What it teaches: a symmetric matrix has three perpendicular eigen-lines, and they are the axes of its ellipsoid.

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: The same eigenvalues as the matrix above (the two differ only by the sign of the off-diagonal entries), but different shapes: for $2 + \sqrt{2}$ the vector is $(-0.50, 0.71, -0.50)$, for $2$ it is $(0.71, 0.00, -0.71)$ and for $2 - \sqrt{2}$ it is $(0.50, 0.71, 0.50)$. These are the normal modes of three masses between walls (see Eigenvalues in Practice (#/math/eigenvalues/applications)). The probe goes to $(1.12, -0.30, 0.39)$, length 1.221, a large $42.1°$ off its line.

Look at the vector for 0.586: all three signs agree, the whole chain swings together, the slowest mode. For 2 the middle mass stays still, for 3.414 neighbours move oppositely, the fastest mode. Set v: direction around to 0° and v: direction up to −45°: v is then on the $\lambda = 2$ line $(0.71, 0.00, -0.71)$ and the readout says '0° off v's line'. What it teaches: frequencies are square roots of eigenvalues, so the lowest mode is the smallest eigenvalue.
Covariance of a data cloud

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: A covariance matrix, symmetric and with positive eigenvalues $4.176$, $0.924$ and $0.5$, along $(0.80, 0.58, 0.16)$, $(-0.56, 0.82, -0.11)$ and $(-0.20, 0.00, 0.98)$. The trace is $5.6$, the total variance, so the first direction carries $74.6\%$ of it. The probe goes to $(3.25, 2.21, 0.78)$, length 4.004, $14.3°$ off.

The green ellipsoid is long and thin: one dominant axis, as in principal component analysis. Press Next step ▶ to step 6 (trace and determinant): the three eigenvalues multiply to $1.93$, the determinant, which is the volume of the image of the unit ball relative to the ball itself. What it teaches: the longest axis is the direction of greatest variance (see Eigenvalues in Practice (#/math/eigenvalues/applications)).

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: A triangular matrix shows its eigenvalues on the diagonal: $3$, $2$ and $1$ (in order of size), with vectors $(0.71, 0.71, 0.00)$, $(1.00, 0.00, 0.00)$ and $(0.41, -0.41, 0.82)$. The matrix is not symmetric and the three lines are not perpendicular: the angles between them are $45.0°$ (the $\lambda = 3$ and $\lambda = 2$ lines), $90.0°$ ($\lambda = 3$ and $\lambda = 1$) and $65.9°$ ($\lambda = 2$ and $\lambda = 1$). One pair happens to be perpendicular, but not all three. The probe goes to $(2.02, 1.78, 0.42)$, length 2.729, $19.4°$ off.

The numbers panel says 'not symmetric'. Step 5 gives the three angles. Turn the view to see that the dashed lines, unlike those of the symmetric matrix, lean on each other, and that the ellipsoid's axes are not on them. What it teaches: no need to solve a cubic for a triangular matrix, since the diagonal is the answer.
Three-state Markov chain

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: A column-stochastic matrix once more: eigenvalues $1$, $0.7$ and $0.4$, the steady state along $(0.57, 0.67, 0.48)$ (that is $(6, 7, 5)/18$ scaled to length 1). This entry starts the probe at v: direction around 0° and v: direction up 0°, so $v = (1, 0, 0)$, certainty in state 1, and the readout gives $Av = (0.80, 0.10, 0.10)$, length 0.812, $10°$ off: the first column of $A$, tomorrow's probabilities.

Powers shown, k is set to 10, and the readout ends 'A^10v = (0.35, 0.38, 0.27), length 0.583': the probabilities after ten steps, near $(0.333, 0.389, 0.278)$. What it teaches: eigenvalue 1 and a steady state, with the others governing how fast it is reached (see Power Iteration and Markov Chains (#/math/eigenvalues/power-iteration)).
Rotation by 60° about the z-axis

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: The axis survives: $\lambda = 1$ along $(0.00, 0.00, 1.00)$, and the other two eigenvalues are the complex pair $0.5 \pm 0.866j$ with $|\lambda| = 1$ and angle $60°$. The amber disc is the plane being turned. The probe goes to $(0.00, 0.91, 0.42)$, length 1, $53.9°$ off. A rotation has $\det = 1$ and trace $1 + 2\cos 60° = 2$, both visible in the numbers panel.

Set Powers shown, k to 6 and the dots go round a circle at constant height, and the sixth coincides with $v$: $A^6 = I$. Set Tilt to its top value, 85°, to look almost straight down the $z$-axis, and the amber disc is nearly a circle. What it teaches: a real 3×3 matrix always has a real eigenvalue, and for a rotation it gives the axis (see Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues)).
Cyclic shift: (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)

widget.title: Cyclic shift: (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0
params.default: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)

blocks.text: Shifting the coordinates round in a ring is a rotation by $120°$ about the diagonal $(1, 1, 1)$. The readout gives $\lambda = 1$ along $(0.58, 0.58, 0.58)$ and $\lambda = -0.5 \pm 0.866j$ ($|\lambda| = 1$, angle $120°$). The probe goes to $(0.42, 0.78, 0.45)$, the same three numbers in a new order, length 1, $28.5°$ off.

Set Powers shown, k to 3. The readout ends 'A^3v = (0.78, 0.45, 0.42)': three shifts bring the coordinates home, $A^3 = I$. The cubic is $\lambda^3 - 1$, with roots the three cube roots of unity: 1 and the pair at $\pm 120°$. What it teaches: this is the same rotation idea in a new place, and the eigenvalues of a shift are roots of unity, the numbers behind the discrete Fourier transform.
Projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

widget.title: Projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0
params.default: projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: The matrix drops each vector onto the plane perpendicular to $(1, 1, 1)$. Every vector already in the plane stays: $\lambda = 1$, a double root with a whole plane of eigenvectors (the blue disc), and the normal direction is crushed, $\lambda = 0$ along $(0.58, 0.58, 0.58)$. The readout says 'λ = 1 (double root), a whole plane of eigenvectors'. The probe goes to $(0.23, -0.10, -0.13)$, length 0.284, $73.5°$ off, since most of it was along the normal.

Look for the difference from the shear chain below: here the repeated eigenvalue 1 has two independent eigenvectors, so the matrix is fine, not defective. The green surface is the flat disc of the image, with no thickness: the determinant is 0. What it teaches: a repeated root can come with a full set of eigenvectors.

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: The worst case: $\lambda = 1$ is a triple root, but there is only one eigen-direction, $(1.00, 0.00, 0.00)$. The readout says 'λ = 1 (triple root), along (1.00, 0.00, 0.00)', and the numbers panel flags the matrix as defective. The probe goes to $(1.24, 0.88, 0.42)$, length 1.574, $10.6°$ off. The determinant is 1: the ellipsoid has the volume of the sphere.

Set Powers shown, k to 10 and see the dots creeping towards the $x$-axis, far more slowly than in any of the other matrices. Press Next step ▶ to step 5, where the text counts the eigenvectors: 'too few'. What it teaches: when roots are repeated the eigenvectors may fall short, and the powers then grow like polynomials, not exponentials (see Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues)).
